extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent practitioners as secondary audience
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claim subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG), including the revised two-prong Step 2A and unchanged Step 2B procedures. Focused on determining whether claims recite judicial exceptions and whether those exceptions are integrated into practical applications or amount to an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim falls within a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No change in 2019 PEG. Example: a claim reciting a series of steps is a process (Step 1 = Yes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised Step 2A — two-prong inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Under revised Step 2A, a claim is eligible at Step 2A unless it (1) recites a judicial exception and (2) the exception is not integrated into a practical application of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no judicial exception is recited (Prong One), claim is eligible and analysis ends. If exception recited but integrated into a practical application (Prong Two), claim is eligible and analysis ends. If recited and not integrated, the claim is 'directed to' the exception and proceed to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identify recitation of a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim recites a judicial exception (an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes recite an exception and determine whether those limitation(s) fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas in the 2019 PEG. For laws of nature/natural phenomena, continue to use the MPEP 'recite' standard (including markedly different characteristics). For abstract ideas, do not use the prior 'Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet'; use the 2019 PEG groupings. Limitations not in the enumerated groupings generally should not be treated as abstract ideas except in rare 'tentative abstract idea' circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupings of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated categories of abstract ideas used in Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2019 PEG groupings include: Mathematical concepts (relationships, formulas, calculations); Mental processes (concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion); Certain methods of organizing human activity (fundamental economic principles/practices including hedging/insurance/mitigating risk; commercial or legal interactions including contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities; managing personal behavior or relationships/interactions between people including social activities, teaching, following rules). Note: Recitation of generic computer components does not necessarily preclude the limitation from being in these groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a judicial exception, determine whether any additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application such that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration requires additional element(s) or combination of elements that apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner imposing a meaningful limit on the exception. Use Supreme Court and Federal Circuit considerations (many found in MPEP 2106.05 subsections) to evaluate integration. If integrated, claim eligible; if not, proceed to Step 2B. Step 2A excludes consideration of well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC) activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: improvements to functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that reflects an improvement to how a computer functions or to any other technology or technical field can indicate integration (Prong Two) or an inventive concept (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Step 2A focus on whether the claim pertains to an improvement to technology (a 'technological solution to a technological problem') without considering whether limitations are WURC. Evaluate whether the specification provides a technical explanation of how to implement the invention and whether the claim itself reflects the improvement. In the streamlined analysis and Step 2B, continue evaluating improvements with reference to whether elements are conventional (MPEP 2106.05(a)). Examples: Enfish (specific data structure that improved computer functionality) vs. Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec (claims did not contain limitations addressing the alleged improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: applying/using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that applies or uses an exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for disease/medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration (expanded after Vanda) applies to treatment/prophylaxis limitations for any judicial exception type. Relevant factors: (a) particularity of the treatment/prophylaxis (must be 'particular' and not generic), (b) whether the limitation has more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception, and (c) whether the limitation is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use. Examples illustrate particular vs. non-particular dosing, applying vs. merely testing, and extra-solution activity vs. steps that alter treatment for subsequent patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: applying the exception with/by a particular machine or manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing or using a judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim can integrate the exception or provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in MPEP 2106.05(b). The machine must be integral and enable a practical application (example: a body temperature detector that takes multiple readings in a particular way to output an accurate core temperature integrates a law of nature into a specific manufacture). Generic invocation of a computer is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: effecting a particular transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can integrate a judicial exception or supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in MPEP 2106.05(c). Example: process steps that change fat and water into free fatty acids and glycerol with specific parameters effect a transformation and practically apply the law of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: other meaningful limitations (meaningful application beyond linking to technology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying/using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking to a technological environment can integrate the exception or supply significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in MPEP 2106.05(e). Example: process steps that meaningfully limit the use of a law of nature to a practical application (e.g., automated rubber press control steps that limit how the natural relationship is applied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations NOT indicative of integration into a practical application (Prong Two negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of additional elements that generally do not integrate an exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: merely adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent); mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea (MPEP 2106.05(f)); adding insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP 2106.05(g)); and generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field-of-use (MPEP 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong Two excludes WURC consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC) activity is not considered in Step 2A Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two even if those elements represent WURC activity. WURC is evaluated only at Step 2B. As a result, a claim that includes WURC elements may still integrate an exception into a practical application at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements: specification must show technical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must provide sufficient details so that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as pertaining to an improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification could identify a technical problem and explain how the specification provides a technical solution. Case examples: McRO v. Bandai (spec explained automation rules for animation tasks), Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (failure to provide details led to ineligibility). After confirming the specification shows an improvement, the claim must reflect that improvement (e.g., claims covering a particular solution rather than merely the idea of a solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — inventive concept ('significantly more') evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is directed to an exception at Step 2A (not integrated), evaluate at Step 2B whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to an inventive concept—i.e., significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: identify additional elements beyond the exception and evaluate them individually and in combination using considerations (improvements, particular machine, transformation, other meaningful limitations, unconventional combination or specific limitations beyond WURC). If claim as a whole amounts to significantly more, claim is eligible; otherwise ineligible. Step 2B continues to consider whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of an inventive concept (Step 2B positives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of claim features indicative of an inventive concept (i.e., 'significantly more').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: improvements to computer functioning or other technology (MPEP 2106.05(a)); applying the exception with/by a particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)); effecting a transformation (MPEP 2106.05(c)); applying the exception in some other meaningful way beyond a mere link to technology (MPEP 2106.05(e) and Vanda); and adding a specific limitation other than what is WURC in the field (MPEP 2106.05(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators that do NOT show an inventive concept (Step 2B negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of claim features that generally do not amount to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: adding 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement on a computer (MPEP 2106.05(f)); adding insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP 2106.05(g)); generally linking to a technological environment (MPEP 2106.05(h)); and appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality (MPEP 2106.05(d) and Berkheimer guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for tentative abstract ideas (non-enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner believes a claim limitation should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings (a 'tentative abstract idea'), follow 2019 PEG-specific steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate under 2019 PEG: if the claim integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application, claim is eligible. Otherwise proceed to Step 2B. If claim fails Step 2B, bring the application to the Technology Center (TC) director. Any rejection treating a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval recorded in the file) and must provide justification for treating the limitation as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting a rejection under 2019 PEG
rubrics_metrics.description: Required content and approach when issuing a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection under the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection should: identify the abstract idea recited in the claim and include a reference to the appropriate enumerated grouping of abstract ideas; identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application; and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept. Use the new form paragraphs where applicable (see form paragraph guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph usage and TC director approval rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions on which 101 form paragraphs to use and when TC director approval is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.05.015 is deleted and replaced by 7.05.016 and 7.05.017. For Step 2B rejections: use existing 7.04.01, 7.05 and new 7.05.016. If the recited judicial exception is an abstract idea not enumerated in the 2019 PEG, use 7.05.016 and 7.05.017 because TC director approval is required. Ensure cross-references and examiner notes are updated appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reminders & substantive practice takeaways
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level examiner guidance to ensure consistent, accurate application of 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the claim as a whole — consider all recited limitations when determining eligibility. Do not use the old 'Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet Identifying Abstract Ideas' for determining whether a claim recites an abstract idea. WURC is considered at Step 2B, not Step 2A. The key inquiry in revised Step 2A is whether a claim reciting a judicial exception is directed to the exception itself or to a practical application of the exception. Practice compact prosecution by addressing all statutory requirements (not just eligibility) and, when possible, point applicants to eligible subject matter in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and reliance on fact patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: How to use USPTO examples (including new examples 37–42) when applying the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New examples 37–42 illustrate 2019 PEG application and should be interpreted based on their specific fact patterns; a claim under examination need not mirror an example claim to be eligible. Existing examples 1–36 were issued prior to the 2019 PEG and may contain analyses not entirely consistent with the 2019 PEG; claims indicated as eligible in prior examples remain eligible but use prior examples with caution. Example analyses highlight application of the groupings, Prong Two considerations, and Step 2B evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applications in process and re-evaluation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How to proceed when applicants respond or when claims were previously rejected under pre-2019 guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant argues claims are eligible, examiners should re-evaluate eligibility of previously rejected claims under the 2019 PEG. If claim is now eligible, withdraw the 101 rejection. If still ineligible, update form paragraphs used and ensure the rejection explains why the claim recites a judicial exception, fails to integrate into a practical application, and fails to provide an inventive concept. Also consider patentability under 102, 103, and 112.
